question: In an Oracle Server Technology round, a C++ candidate was asked OOP questions: how many types of polymorphism there are; what an abstract class is, how it is made and why; what an interface is and how it differs from an abstract class; if a derived class defines a function with the same name and number of parameters as a virtual base function but a different parameter type, is it still overriding; and what happens if you call a derived-class (overridden) function through a base class object.
lookingFor: Clear definition of compile-time versus run-time polymorphism
Understanding of virtual functions, vtables and pure virtual functions
Knowing the exact rules for overriding versus hiding and overloading
Understanding of object slicing and why dispatch needs a pointer or reference
Distinguishing an abstract class from an interface
answer:
**Types of polymorphism.** Compile-time (static): function overloading, operator overloading and templates, resolved by the compiler. Run-time (dynamic): virtual functions, where the function called depends on the actual object type, resolved through the vtable.

**Abstract class.** A class with at least one pure virtual function (`virtual double area() const = 0;`). It cannot be instantiated and exists to define a contract that derived classes (`Rectangle`, `Triangle`) must implement. It can also hold data members and implemented functions. Declare a virtual destructor in any base class meant to be used polymorphically.

**Interface vs abstract class.** C++ has no `interface` keyword; an interface is a class with only pure virtual functions and no state. In Java, an interface declares capabilities a class can implement (multiple allowed), while an abstract class can hold state and partial implementation but a class can extend only one. Use an interface for a capability, an abstract class for shared base behavior.

**Same name, different parameter type.** This is not overriding. Overriding requires the same name and the same parameter list (and compatible return type, plus const-ness). With a different parameter type you have declared a new function that hides the base version (name hiding), and no virtual dispatch happens for it. Marking it `override` makes the compiler reject it, which is why you should always write `override`.

**Calling through a base object.** Dynamic dispatch needs a base pointer or reference to a derived object. If you have a base-type object, you always get the base version, since the object is a base; assigning a derived object to a base variable slices off the derived part. So `Base b = derived; b.f();` calls `Base::f`. Calling a function that exists only in the derived class through a base pointer or object is a compile error, because the base type has no such member. (The write-up reported "error" for this case; that is only true for the second situation.)

```cpp
Base* p = new Derived();
p->f();   // Derived::f, since f is virtual
```
